_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-include-verses-placement-proposal-v1-20261008.md:113 > A plan can also be held against someone's good without anyone calling it a plot. Joab knew *"that the king's heart went out to Absalom"* (2 Samuel 14:1). He sent a wise woman of Tekoa with a staged plea, and *"put the words in her mouth"* (14:3). In it she told David that by leaving Absalom in exile he had *"planned such a thing against the people of God"* (14:13). Beside it she set God, who *"devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast"* (14:14). David saw whose plan it was: *"Is the hand of Joab with you in all this?"* (14:19). Three are at work in the one passage: Joab's scheme, the king's planning, and God's devising as she declares it. The king's planning is measured against God's (13.1, *Purposing*).

new.text: The looking-ahead words are used most often against another person. It is placed in the heart: "let none of you devise evil against another in your heart" (Zec 7:10), "do not devise evil in your hearts against one another" (Zec 8:17). It is done together: "Come, let us make plots against Jeremiah" (Jer 18:18); "In Heshbon they planned disaster against her" (Jer 48:2); "they made plans to put him to death" (Joh 11:53), and Lazarus as well (Joh 12:10); "The soldiers’ plan was to kill the prisoners" (Act 27:42). It is aimed at the righteous and the weak: "The wicked plots against the righteous and gnashes his teeth at him" (Psa 37:12); "who have planned to trip up my feet" (Psa 140:4). It hides behind a friendly word: "Come and let us meet together" "But they intended to do me harm" (Neh 6:2); Saul's bride-price, "Saul thought to make David fall by the hand of the Philistines" (1Sa 18:25). It is pinned on the other side: "you and the Jews intend to rebel" (Neh 6:6). Another pleads against it: Esther "pleaded with him to avert the evil plan of Haman" (Est 8:3; 9:24).
new.meaning: Looking ahead in these verses is mostly turned against another: devised in the heart, done together, aimed at the righteous and the weak, covered by a friendly word, and met by the plea of another.
new.setting: Psalms, prophets, Nehemiah, Esther, Samuel, Daniel, John and Acts.
new.implication: The plotter's power and the outcome are not the same: "though they devise mischief, they will not succeed" (Psa 21:11); "do not further their evil plot" (Psa 140:8).
new.parties: the wicked and the righteous; Jeremiah's opponents; the council; Sanballat and Geshem; Saul and David; Haman and Esther; kings of Daniel 11; the soldiers in Acts 27

new.text: Looking ahead weighs before it acts: a king "will not sit down first and deliberate whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand" (Luk 14:31); "She considers a field and buys it" (Pro 31:16); "consider it, take counsel, and speak" (Judg 19:30). It plans without knowing: "on the chance that somehow they could reach Phoenix" (Act 27:12), "supposing that they had obtained their purpose" (Act 27:13), "they planned if possible to run the ship ashore" (Act 27:39). A plan carries a word: "Do I make my plans according to the flesh, ready to say Yes, yes and No, no at the same time?" (2Co 1:17). Plans part people: "Barnabas wanted to take with them John called Mark" (Act 15:37); Joseph of Arimathea "had not consented to their decision and action" (Luk 23:51). And a plan can be for another's good: "because an excellent spirit was in him. And the king planned to set him over the whole kingdom" (Dan 6:3).
new.meaning: The capacity to look ahead weighs ability and cost first, plans under uncertainty, binds one's word, can part companions or set one apart from a council, and can plan another's good.
new.setting: Luke 14 and 23, Proverbs 31, Judges 19, Acts 15 and 27, 2 Corinthians 1, Daniel 6.
new.implication: The plan in Dan 6:3 rests on what the king saw in Daniel's spirit.
new.parties: the king going to war; the capable wife; Israel after Gibeah; the sailors; Paul; Barnabas and Paul; Joseph of Arimathea; Darius and Daniel

file_lines: _analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-will-reading-v1-20261008.md:114 - **Wanting to know.** *"desiring to know the real reason"* (Act 22:30; 23:28); *"We wish to know therefore what these things mean"* (Act 17:20); *"I would like to hear the man myself"* (Act 25:22); Daniel, *"I desired to know the truth about the fourth beast"* (Dan 7:19).

new.text: The will word also carries wanting to know and stated wishes: "desiring to know the real reason" (Act 22:30; 23:28); "We wish to know therefore what these things mean" (Act 17:20); "I would like to hear the man myself" (Act 25:22); "I refuse to be a judge of these things" (Act 18:15). Paul's wishes in teaching each come with their reason: "I desire then that in every place the men should pray, lifting holy hands without anger or quarreling" (1Ti 2:8); "So I would have younger widows marry" (1Ti 5:14); "I want you to insist on these things, so that those who have believed in God may be careful to devote themselves to good works" (Tit 3:8); "I want you to know" (Phi 1:12); "so that our joy may be complete" (2Jo 12); "I want to remind you" (Jude 5).
new.meaning: The Greek will word also names a desire to know, a refusal of a role, and a teacher's stated wish, each given its reason.
new.setting: Acts 17, 18, 22, 23 and 25; the letters; slight bearing on the inner being for several (the will reading, route).
new.implication: A stated wish in teaching is weaker evidence for the inner act than a wish in narrative.
new.parties: the tribune; the Athenians; Agrippa; Gallio; Paul; John; Jude

items.text: Now I want to remind you, although you once fully knew it, that Jesus, who saved a people out of the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe.
